profile.campus: QTS Fayetteville campus, 13 buildings, approximately 6.2 million sq ft, along Highway 54 West between Veterans Parkway and Tyrone Road
profile.reading:
Per Data Center Dynamics' 2022 reporting (confirming QTS as the buyer behind a previously unnamed mega-project), QTS acquired 600 acres in Fayette County, roughly 20 miles south of Atlanta, for $153.8 million ($250,000/acre); the planned campus is designed for 250MW of capacity across 1.5 million sq ft of building space, with QTS expected to invest more than $1 billion developing the site. A Baxtel listing gives 1435 Hwy 54 W, Fayetteville, GA as the campus address. The land was previously farmland that had also drawn interest from Oceanic Data Centers (approved 2020) and Facebook (which considered the site in 2018 before choosing Newton County, Georgia instead).

QTS was founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas, and was taken private in a roughly $10 billion Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT)-led acquisition completed August 31, 2021, per Blackstone's own press release; QTS is no longer an independent SEC filer. QTS's own site lists an operations support center in Suwanee, Georgia, making this Atlanta-metro cluster (Atlanta proper, Suwanee/Gwinnett County, and Fayetteville/Fayette County) an operationally significant hub for the company beyond its Northern Virginia headquarters.

Georgia Power, the state's dominant investor-owned electric utility, has flagged data center load growth in its own integrated resource plan filings with state regulators as a major driver of future generation and transmission investment, a pattern also seen among Northern Virginia's Dominion Energy and Texas's ERCOT grid operator elsewhere in this registry. Metro Atlanta's data center growth has also drawn legislative attention over sales-tax exemptions for data center equipment, a policy debate covered in Georgia trade and political press as the industry has expanded across Fulton, Gwinnett, Fayette, and neighboring counties.

profile.campus_note: One of 4 buildings OpenStreetMap contributors have mapped under this name in this locality, numbered west to east.
profile.capacity_note: The 6.2 million square feet is the campus total across thirteen buildings as stated by the City of Fayetteville, not the floor area of this building. QTS publishes no per-building figure for the campus and no IT capacity figure at all, so none is recorded here. Four of the thirteen buildings are mapped in OpenStreetMap and appear separately in this registry.
profile.facility_note: QTS Fayetteville, Georgia: a planned 600-acre, 250MW, 1.5M sq ft mega-campus, over $1 billion in expected investment, on land Facebook once considered before choosing Newton County.
profile.research_note:
Gap-view review: this is one of several rows tracking QTS's planned (not-yet-built) Fayette County, GA megacampus (600 acres, planned 250MW/1.5M sqft total per Data Center Dynamics 2022 reporting); no per-building figures exist for this pre-construction site, and no per-building breakout is published for however many buildings will comprise the eventual campus. No numeric key written.

[2026-09-05, Claude] Campus facts from the City of Fayetteville data centre FAQ. The city states one campus, thirteen buildings, approximately 6.2 million sq ft, on Highway 54 West between Veterans Parkway and Tyrone Road. Four buildings are mapped in OpenStreetMap and carry this shared campus record; the other nine are not mapped. No per-building floor area or IT capacity is published by QTS or the city, so none is stored. The prohibition on new data centres, Ordinance 26-O-12 of 5 March 2026, is recorded because it is a fact about the site regulatory setting, not a judgement about it.
profile.community_note: Fayetteville publishes a data centre FAQ that answers residents in the state's own terms rather than the industry's: it cites the Congressional Research Service on what a data centre is and why it draws power, and the Georgia Public Service Commission on rates. The Commission ordered a freeze of Georgia Power base rates through 2028 on 31 July 2025, and states that it is working to prevent new data centres from shifting costs to residential customers. A city that hosts 6.2 million square feet of data centre and has since prohibited any more is a useful case: the record of both decisions is public and sits on the same page.
profile.incentives_note: The city states that QTS project estimates put the campus at $150 million to $200 million a year in real property tax revenue and about $170 million in sales tax revenue, supporting several hundred ongoing operational jobs alongside construction and indirect employment. Those are QTS estimates relayed by the city rather than assessed collections.
profile.regulatory_note: No further data centre may be built in Fayetteville. On 5 March 2026 the City Council adopted Ordinance 26-O-12, amending chapters 200 and 400 of the Unified Development Ordinance to prohibit data centres in every City of Fayetteville zoning district. The QTS campus predates the prohibition and is unaffected by it; the ordinance closes the city to any new development of this kind.
profile.planned_capacity: Planned project: could extend to 250 MW and 1.5 million sq ft at full build-out on 600 acres (per Data Center Dynamics trade press); this is planned/future capacity, not confirmed current operating capacity, and is a project total not a per-building figure.
profile.regional_context: QTS was founded 2003, HQ Overland Park KS, acquired by Blackstone for ~$10B in 2021.
profile.facility_type_note: Part of QTS's Atlanta-area campus, spanning Atlanta proper, Fayette County, and Gwinnett County, Georgia. Georgia (Atlanta) was one of QTS's earliest markets, per Wikipedia's account of the company's 2005-2007 acquisition-driven expansion.

reading.body:
QTS acquired 600 acres in Fayette County, Georgia, roughly 20 miles south of Atlanta, in 2022 for $153.8 million. The company has announced a planned campus of 250 MW capacity across 1.5 million square feet of building space, with expected total investment exceeding $1 billion. The campus is designed as a 13-building project, though no per-building capacity figures are published and construction has not reached the phase where building-level specifications are confirmed.

No operating capacity at this campus is published. The campus remains in the planned or early acquisition phase, not yet generating measurable IT load. Until buildings become operational and their power draw is measured or disclosed, this site contributes zero megawatts to Georgia's current data center footprint or the grid's binding constraint on AI scaling.

If built to specification, the Fayetteville campus would rank as Georgia's largest published data center project by a substantial margin. Georgia Power has flagged data center load growth as a major driver of future generation and transmission investment in its regulatory filings. The state currently shows 66.3 megawatts of published capacity across four facilities with confirmed figures; this 250 MW project would represent a more than threefold increase in announced AI-accessible capacity.
